title: There Is Another Hand
bodyHtml:
Most languages spoken in Europe today are Indo-European, brought to Europe by waves of migration 3000 to 8000 years ago. Before this, various other languages were spoken, such as the language of Minoan Crete, famous for its undeciphered writing system known as Linear A. Of these old European languages, only Basque survives, being spoken by around 800,000 people in northern Spain and southern France.

In the same way that French and Spanish descend from Latin, modern-day Basque descends from an older language called Proto-Basque. Although there are no speakers of Proto-Basque left, linguists can use historical methods to attempt to reconstruct what words in Proto-Basque may have looked like. For example, here is one proposal for the Proto-Basque numbers 1–9, given in a random order. Note that since these words are reconstructed, rather than known for certain, they are preceded by *.

A. *bada-eriB. *berr-eri-ahurC. *atz-az-berr-eri
D. *be-oro-atzE. *berr-eriF. *atz-az-bada-eri-ahur-itzi
G. *atz-az-berr-eri-ahur-itziH. *atz-az-eriI. *eri-ahur

Each of the Proto-Basque numbers are made of smaller word-parts, with meanings related to counting on your hand. For example, *berr-eri literally means another finger.

Below are the word-parts of Proto-Basque numbers, with their English translations given in a random order. Note that the meanings of *be and *itzi are not relevant (linguists have other reasons to believe that they were present).

Proto-Basque word-parts:

  • i. *ahur
  • ii. *atz
  • iii. *az
  • iv. *bada
  • v. *berr
  • vi. *eri
  • vii. *oro

English translations (random order):

  • J. another
  • K. finger
  • L. hand
  • M. (in) palm (of hand)
  • N. there is
  • O. with
  • P. whole

Later in the problem you will also need the modern Basque numbers 5–10 in a northern dialect, given again in a random order:

Q. zazpiR. bortzS. zortzi
T. bederatziU. hamarV. sei

assets.alt: Five line drawings of a right hand, showing in turn one finger raised, two fingers raised, three fingers raised with two folded into the palm, four fingers raised with the thumb folded, and all five fingers spread open.

questions.partPrompt: Determine the correct correspondences between the Proto-Basque words A to I and the numbers from 1 to 9.
Determine the correct correspondences between the Proto-Basque word-parts i. to vii. and their English translations J to P. Answer with the letter.

Determine which number from 5 to 10 each of the modern Basque numbers Q to V means. It may be helpful to know that the Basque z is very similar to s (although pronounced with the tongue touching the teeth), and that p and b are similar consonants.

hints.text: You are given one translation for free: *berr-eri means 'another finger'. That already pins down two word-parts. Now sort the nine Proto-Basque words into groups by which chunks they share — notice that four of them begin with exactly the same two pieces, and one of them contains no *eri at all.

These numbers are built by counting on one hand: small numbers name fingers, and once the hand is used up, the bigger numbers are 'hand with (small number)'. So the words that begin *atz-az- are the numbers above five, and what follows *atz-az- is (almost) the word for the number you add to five. Word length generally grows with the number, too.

Here is the method on an invented form. Suppose Proto-Basque had *atz-az-atz. Stripping off the *atz-az- prefix ('hand with') leaves *atz 'hand', which is five, so the whole thing would mean five plus five, i.e. ten. Use exactly this stripping-and-adding step on the real *atz-az- words, and for the modern Basque forms match beginnings and endings letter by letter (remembering z≈s and p≈b).

explanationHtml:
Step 1: use the free translation

The problem tells you that *berr-eri literally means another finger. Since the word-parts are written in the same order as the English, that gives you two pieces straight away: *berr = another (J) and *eri = finger (K).

And what number is 'another finger'? If you count on your hand, the first finger is number one, and 'another finger' is the next one: two. So E = 2.

Step 2: group the nine words by shape

Line the nine words up and look at what they share:

  • Four words begin with *atz-az-: C, F, G, H.
  • One word contains no *eri 'finger' at all: D *be-oro-atz.
  • Four words contain *eri but no *atz-az-: A, B, E, I.

That 4 + 1 + 4 split is a huge clue, because a hand has five fingers. The four 'finger-only' words are 1–4 (counting fingers), D is 5 (the whole hand is used up), and the four *atz-az- words are 6–9 ('hand with ...').

Step 3: sort out 1 to 4

We know E *berr-eri = 2. Of the remaining three:

  • A *bada-eri is the simplest 'X finger' word left, and 1 is the simplest number: A = 1. (The title of the problem, There Is Another Hand, is a nudge: *bada = there is, so 1 is literally 'there is a finger'.)
  • B *berr-eri-ahur is E (=2) plus one more piece, *ahur, so it should be the next number up: B = 3.
  • That leaves I *eri-ahur = 4.

Look at the hand pictures: in the drawings for 3 and 4 some fingers are folded down into the palm. That fits *ahur = (in) palm (of hand) (M), appearing exactly in 3 and 4 (and later in 8 and 9).

Step 4: sort out 6 to 9

Strip *atz-az- off each of C, F, G, H and see what number is left over:

Wordafter stripping *atz-az-that piece is...5 + it =
H *atz-az-eri*erione finger → 16
C *atz-az-berr-eri*berr-eri= E = 27
G *atz-az-berr-eri-ahur-itzi*berr-eri-ahur (+*itzi)= B = 38
F *atz-az-bada-eri-ahur-itzi*bada-eri-ahur (+*itzi)the 4-type 'fingers in palm' word9

Notice that this also confirms Step 3: the tail of the 8-word is exactly the word for 3, which only works if B (not I) is 3. The words also get steadily longer as the numbers get bigger, another good check.

Step 5: finish the word-part meanings (H2)

  • *eri = finger (K), *berr = another (J) — given.
  • *ahur = (in) palm (of hand) (M) — it marks the numbers where fingers are folded into the palm.
  • *bada = there is (N) — it opens the word for 1, 'there is a finger'.
  • The prefix *atz-az- must mean 'hand with', and *atz also appears in D, the word for 5. So *atz = hand (L) and *az = with (O).
  • That leaves *oro = whole (P), which makes D *be-oro-atz literally '(the) whole hand' — a perfect name for 5.

Step 6: the modern Basque numbers (H3)

Now compare each modern word with the reconstructions, using the two sound tips: z is basically an s, and p and b are near-twins. Words change over thousands of years mostly by losing bits and smoothing sounds, so look for surviving beginnings and endings.

  • bederatzi (T): starts bede- like *bada-, has an r from *eri, and ends -atzi like *-itzi. That is F, so 9.
  • zortzi (S): also ends in -tzi, the other *-itzi word, and begins with a z from *atz-az-. Since 9 is taken, this is G, 8.
  • zazpi (Q): zaz- is a squashed *atz-az-, and the p comes from the b of *berr. That is C, 7.
  • sei (V): short, with just an s (≈ z from *atz-az) and the -i remnant of *eri. That is H, 6.
  • bortz (R): b...or...tz lines up piece for piece with *be-oro-atz. That is D, 5.
  • hamar (U) is left over, and indeed it resembles none of the reconstructions — because no Proto-Basque word for 10 was given. So it is 10.

The nice moral: modern Basque 5–9 still carry, in worn-down form, the ancient sentence-like descriptions of counting on one hand.

The official solution gives no per-item point breakdown, so the 15 points were split as H1 = 6.3 (0.7 x 9), H2 = 4.2 (0.6 x 7), H3 = 4.5 (0.75 x 6); adjust if the official marking scheme differs.
